title: 528. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Transitive Relations
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: State the definition of a transitive relation.
questions.question: When is a relation \(R\) on a set \(A\) transitive?

options.label: A
options.text: When \((a,b)\in R\) and \((b,c)\in R\) together imply \((a,c)\in R\)

questions.explanation: A relation is transitive when any two pairs that link up, \((a,b)\) followed by \((b,c)\), always produce the direct pair \((a,c)\). The condition "\((a,b)\in R\) implies \((b,a)\in R\)" defines symmetry.
questions.hint: Transitivity concerns chains of two pairs.

questions.learningObjective: Decide which relation on a small set is transitive.
questions.question: Which relation on \(\{1,2,3\}\) is transitive?
questions.explanation: In the first relation the only chain is \((1,2)\) followed by \((2,3)\), and the required pair \((1,3)\) is present. In the second relation the same chain occurs, but \((1,3)\) is missing, so it is not transitive.
questions.hint: Find every chain \((a,b)\), \((b,c)\) and check for the pair \((a,c)\).

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether the relation less than is transitive.
questions.question: Is the relation \(<\) on the real numbers transitive?
questions.explanation: If \(a\) is less than \(b\) and \(b\) is less than \(c\), then \(a\) is less than \(c\); this is a basic property of the order of real numbers. The falsity of \(a<a\) concerns reflexivity and does not affect transitivity.
questions.hint: Test only the condition for transitivity.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether perpendicularity of lines in a plane is transitive.
questions.question: On the set of lines in a plane, is the relation "is perpendicular to" transitive?

options.label: A
options.text: No; if \(\ell\perp m\) and \(m\perp n\), then \(\ell\) is parallel to \(n\) or equal to \(n\), not perpendicular to it.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; if \(\ell\perp m\) and \(m\perp n\), then \(\ell\perp n\).

questions.explanation: Two lines in a plane that are both perpendicular to the same line have the same direction. So from \(\ell\perp m\) and \(m\perp n\) it follows that \(\ell\) and \(n\) are parallel or coincide, and they are not perpendicular. The relation is therefore not transitive.
questions.hint: Think of the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-axis, and a horizontal line.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether the relation not equal to is transitive.
questions.question: Is the relation \(a\ne b\) on the integers transitive?

options.label: B
options.text:
Yes; if \(a
e b\) and \(b
e c\), then \(a
e c\).

questions.explanation:
Transitivity must hold for all choices, including \(c=a\). With \(a=1\), \(b=2\), \(c=1\): \(1
e 2\) and \(2
e 1\) are true, but \(1
e 1\) is false. So the relation is not transitive.
questions.hint: Try a chain that returns to its starting element.

questions.learningObjective: Find the pair missing from an almost transitive relation.
questions.question: Which ordered pair must be added to \(\{(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(1,3),(2,4)\}\) to make the relation transitive?
questions.explanation: The chain \((1,2)\), \((2,4)\) requires \((1,4)\), and so does the chain \((1,3)\), \((3,4)\); that pair is missing. After adding \((1,4)\), every chain has its direct pair. The pair \((4,1)\) points in the wrong direction and is not required by any chain.
questions.hint: Combine the pairs that link up and list the direct pairs they require.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a relation consisting of a pair and its reversal is transitive.
questions.question: Is the relation \(\{(1,2),(2,1)\}\) on \(\{1,2\}\) transitive?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; it contains every pair of different elements.

options.label: B
options.text: No; the chain \((1,2)\), \((2,1)\) requires \((1,1)\), which is missing.

questions.explanation: The pairs \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) link up, so transitivity requires \((1,1)\); similarly \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\) require \((2,2)\). Neither is present, so the relation is not transitive.
questions.hint: A chain may end where it started; check what pair that requires.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether inclusion of sets is transitive.
questions.question: Is the relation \(\subseteq\) on the subsets of a set \(S\) transitive?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes; if \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\), then every element of \(A\) is in \(C\).

options.label: B
options.text: No; \(A\subseteq B\) and \(B\subseteq C\) do not relate \(A\) to \(C\).

questions.explanation: If every element of \(A\) is in \(B\), and every element of \(B\) is in \(C\), then every element of \(A\) is in \(C\). So \(A\subseteq C\), and the relation is transitive.
questions.hint: Follow one element of \(A\) through the two inclusions.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a relation with a single pair is transitive.
questions.question: Is the relation \(R=\{(1,2)\}\) on \(\{1,2,3\}\) transitive?

options.label: A
options.text: No; the pairs \((2,3)\) and \((1,3)\) are missing.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes; there are no pairs \((a,b)\) and \((b,c)\) in \(R\) that link up, so the condition holds vacuously.

questions.explanation: Transitivity requires \((a,c)\in R\) only when both \((a,b)\in R\) and \((b,c)\in R\). The only pair is \((1,2)\), and no pair starts with \(2\), so no chain exists. With nothing to check, the relation is transitive. Transitivity never forces pairs such as \((2,3)\) to be present on their own.
questions.hint: Look for two pairs of \(R\) in which the second component of one equals the first component of the other.

questions.learningObjective: Count the pairs in the smallest transitive relation containing a given relation.
questions.question: How many ordered pairs are in the smallest transitive relation that contains \(\{(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)\}\)?
questions.explanation: The chains \((1,2),(2,3)\) and \((2,3),(3,4)\) require \((1,3)\) and \((2,4)\). Then \((1,3),(3,4)\) requires \((1,4)\). The result is \(\{(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(1,3),(2,4),(1,4)\}\), with \(6\) pairs. Stopping after the first round of additions gives only \(5\) pairs and is not yet transitive.
questions.hint: After adding the pairs required by existing chains, check whether new chains have appeared.
